blog.title: Migrating Messenger storage to optimize performance

pageTitle: Moving a billion chats to a new shelf
summary: Facebook says it moved Messenger's stored messages from HBase to MyRocks, a MySQL-based database, without downtime. The company reports it needed 90 percent less storage and read latency is 50 times lower.

hook.teaser: How do you move a billion chat histories to a new database while people keep chatting?

blocks.kicker: Distributed systems / A picture story in four parts
blocks.title: Moving Messenger's shelves

chapters.title: Moving a whole library while it is open
chapters.caption: Messenger started as something like email: messages waited in your inbox. Today it is a live chat system, and Facebook says more than a billion people use it. The team wanted to move all the stored messages to a new kind of database. But the app could not close for the day. And some businesses keep chats open all day and night.

media.alt: A busy library where readers keep walking in and out while movers carry boxes of books to a new building across the road.

chapters.title: Swap the shelves, not the readers
chapters.caption: The post says the team had used HBase since 2010. It moved the messages to MyRocks, Facebook's own database that puts RocksDB inside MySQL. It also moved from spinning disks to flash storage. The team says MySQL's way of making copies fits how its data centers already run, so it could keep fewer copies.

media.alt: An old slow shelf with spinning wheels beside a new shelf with a lightning bolt. A librarian points at the new shelf.

chapters.title: Two ways to move people
chapters.caption: Most accounts went the normal way: a quiet moment, copy everything, check nothing changed, then write to both systems and compare. Busy accounts, like big business bots, went the buffered way. The team copied a snapshot into a holding area, and new messages waited in a queue called Iris. Then the new system caught up.

media.alt: Two lanes into a new building. A short lane with a quiet door for most people, and a long lane with a waiting room where a line of messages queues up.

chapters.title: What Facebook says it got
chapters.caption: Facebook reports that all accounts moved: 99.9 percent in two weeks by the normal way, the rest two weeks later. It says storage use fell by 90 percent without data loss, and read latency is now 50 times lower. These are the company's own numbers, not tested by anyone else. See "Benefits of the new system" ↗

media.alt: A scoreboard with three plain boards: 90 percent less storage, six copies down to three, and reads 50 times faster, each with a small drawing.

strips.title: Why move at all?
strips.grownUpWords: HBase, MyRocks, key-value store, MySQL storage engine

panels.caption: Messenger's messages lived in HBase, a big shelf for notes. The post says it served the team well from 2010.

media.alt: A big wooden shelf full of folders with a worn label that says since 2010.

panels.caption: The post says HBase work is bound by disk reads. The team says that made some features hard, like searching messages on a phone.

media.alt: A tired librarian runs back and forth between shelves with a long queue of folders. A speech bubble says: too slow to search.

panels.caption: So the team chose MyRocks: a new shelf built into MySQL. The post says phone message search then became possible.

media.alt: A neat new shelf with a lightning bolt. A phone beside it shows a magnifying glass finding a message.

strips.title: Flash and fewer copies
strips.grownUpWords: flash storage, replication factor, compression, Zstandard

panels.caption: The old shelves sat on spinning disks. The new ones sit on flash, which has no moving parts.

media.alt: A spinning disk crossed out on the left, a small flat flash card with a sparkle on the right.

panels.caption: The post says the new design was smaller on disk. A squeezing method called Zstandard saved even more space.

media.alt: A folder gets squeezed by a clamp into a thin folder, with a small zip on it.

panels.caption: And the team says it could keep three copies of the data instead of six. In total, the post says storage use fell by 90 percent.

media.alt: Six stacked folders on the left, three on the right, with a happy accountant holding a clipboard.

strips.title: The normal way
strips.grownUpWords: state machine, double-writing, validation, revert plan

panels.caption: Each account is in one of a few states: not moved, double-writing, or done. While it moves, nobody may write to it.

media.alt: Three signs on a path: Not moved, Both shelves, Done. A small figure walks along it carrying a folder.

panels.caption: The team copies the history, then checks whether anything new arrived. If it did, the move fails, the copy is wiped, and a later job tries again.

media.alt: A librarian compares a counter before and after copying. The numbers differ, and the librarian shakes a head and sweeps the new copy away.

panels.caption: In double-writing, every new message goes to both shelves, and the team compares them. If something is wrong, the account can roll back.

media.alt: Two shelves side by side, a folder going into each, and a magnifying glass comparing them. A big undo arrow sits below.

panels.caption: Some accounts, like a business bot, get messages all the time. There is no quiet moment to move them.

media.alt: A bot at a desk with a never-ending stream of letters flowing in. A clock has no quiet hour.

panels.caption: So the team takes a snapshot at a cutoff time and copies it into a holding room first. The post says that copy takes about a tenth of the migration time.

media.alt: A camera flashes at a pile of folders. The photo goes into a holding room.

panels.caption: Meanwhile new messages wait in a queue called Iris. The post says it can hold them for weeks. Then the new system catches up.

media.alt: A long line of letters waits in a tube marked Iris. A new shelf at the end takes them one by one.

panels.caption: A tool called Bistro, another Facebook open source project, schedules the jobs. It can also slow them down if something looks wrong.

media.alt: A traffic officer with a dial that goes from slow to fast, directing small trucks of folders.

panels.caption: Then new accounts are made only on the new system, and writing to HBase stops, one cluster at a time.

media.alt: A row of old shelves with the lights going off one by one. New accounts walk to the new shelf.

panels.caption: Last, an accounting job checks that no account was left behind. Then the old system went offline.

media.alt: A librarian ticks a long checklist. The old building has a closed sign on the door.

panels.caption: The post says reading is now much faster. Scrolling back through old messages feels quicker.

media.alt: A phone with a scrolling chat and little speed lines. A happy user thumbs up.

panels.caption: The team says it also made switching to another data center much faster, with no people doing manual steps.

media.alt: Two buildings joined by a bridge. A big switch flips by itself while a worker sips tea.

panels.caption: It also let Messenger reuse Facebook's search system built on MySQL, so searching old chats works on the phone too.

media.alt: A phone with a search box and a magnifying glass finding one message in a long chat.
